newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan executives seek Japan deregulation.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan executives seek Japan deregulation.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese business leaders agreed on the need to deregulate Japan's economy, as they began a meeting on Tuesday to discuss trade between the two economic giants.
About 200 business executives from Japan and the United States attended the two-day U.S.-Japan business conference in San Francisco.

The delegates, including a number of top executives of Japanese and U.S. multinationals, discussed deregulation and market access, exchange rates and the role of the United States and Japan in Asia at the annual meeting of the U.S.-Japan and Japan-U.S. business councils.
Westinghouse Electric Corp Chairman Michael Jordan, the chairman of the U.S.-Japan Business Council, was blunt about what measures he believed Japan had to take to kickstart its economy.
"Most of us here on the U.S. side strongly believe that Japan needs to deregulate and deregulate deeply and quickly for its own good," he told the conference.

"The recent decline in the yen against the dollar seems to have convinced some that Japan can export its way back to prosperity, but a short-term rise in the bilateral trade deficit makes it difficult for Americans to grasp why Japan has not done more to fix its economy," he said.
U.S. government officials have recently voiced concern at a sharp rise in Japan's trade surplus.

However, Jordan said Americans were impressed that deregulation of the Japanese economy was "now on the front burner." "Deregulation will do wonders for domestic demand in Japan, thus perhaps blunting the need for a fierce export war again," he said.

Shoichiro Toyoda, chairman of Toyota Motor Corp, said the Japanese were beginning to recognize that excessive regulation imposed a heavy cost on their industries. "So momentum is building for reform," he told the conference.

"Formerly, deregulation and market-opening measures in Japan usually have been in response to foreign pressure. But things have changed. Now, we must take the initiative in undertaking reform because it is in our own best interests," said Toyoda, who is also chairman of the Keidanren, the Japan Federation of Economic Organizations.

He tried to reassure the Americans over Japan's growing trade surplus, saying the surplus was unlikely "over the medium and long terms to expand as it has in the past" provided that there was a stable yen/dollar exchange rate.

But Wayne Booker, vice chairman of Ford Motor Co, voiced concern at a rise in Japanese auto exports to the United States over the last six months, telling reporters he believed this was partly due to the recent weakening of the yen.

Representatives of Japanese and U.S. manufacturing industries who met separately at the meeting on Tuesday agreed on the desirability of a stable yen-dollar exchange rate, delegates said. The conference ends on Wednesday.
